passage:
Dear Seema,
I need to tell someone this. Every evening I post a photo and then check the likes like a pulse. Yesterday my sketch got nine, and I felt as though I had done something wrong. Then I saw that my classmates' posts had hundreds, and I spent the whole night refreshing. My chest felt tight and I couldn't focus on chemistry.
This morning I noticed the loop: post, check, feel low, post again. So I muted three accounts that always make me feel less, and I'll only share a drawing if I still like it, not because I need a number. Can I send you my next one instead? I miss our summer evenings drawing in the courtyard 🙂
Your Leela

qa.q: How many likes did Leela's sketch get yesterday?
qa.a: Leela's sketch got nine likes.

qa.q: Why did nine likes make Leela feel so low?
qa.a: The few likes felt like a verdict on Leela's worth, bringing a low, anxious feeling and a whole night of refreshing.

qa.q: What could Leela try if the urge to check likes returns?
qa.a: Leela could remember the loop of posting, checking and feeling low, keep the accounts muted, and post only drawings Leela still likes, for personal reasons.

qa.q: How might Seema feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Seema may feel trusted and a little worried, and glad to be asked for the next drawing, since Leela is reaching out to a person rather than to the likes.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing the post-and-check loop of likes and choosing personal reasons to post and muting accounts.

passage:
Tuesday: Devika opened the app for one quick look at a cooking clip. Ninety minutes later she was still there, watching strangers shout at each other, each video angrier than the last, her jaw tight. Her homework sat untouched.
Friday: Manjula noticed her friend's puffy eyes. "You keep saying the app knows what you like. I think it knows what keeps you." Devika frowned, then admitted that whenever she paused on an upsetting clip, more of them came.
The next Wednesday: Devika set a daily limit, unfollowed the angry pages and followed two pottery makers. When the reminder buzzed, she put the phone in a drawer and helped her mother chop onions.

qa.q: What did Devika follow after she unfollowed the angry pages?
qa.a: She followed two pottery makers.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as the clips got angrier, and what tells you?
qa.a: She was getting tense and upset, shown by her tight jaw, yet she kept watching because each clip pulled her to the next.

qa.q: Why do Devika's steps suit an app built to hold attention?
qa.a: Setting a daily limit, curating what she follows and stepping away when the reminder buzzed all cut down how much the feed can keep serving her.

qa.q: How might Manjula have seen the change in Devika?
qa.a: Manjula noticed the puffy eyes and explained gently, so probably felt worried at first and relieved to see Devika take control.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising a feed designed for attention and setting limits and curating follows.

passage:
My thumb still twitches, Ayesha, that's how bad it got. I'm Kavitha, and last month I glanced at my phone every couple of minutes, in class, at dinner, even in the bathroom. Because what if the group planned something and I missed it?
Then Amma took the phone for the evening at my aunt's wedding, and I sat there itching, sure the whole world was moving on without me. Nobody moved on. Honestly, nobody even messaged.
The next week I turned off every notification except calls, and I told you, just ring me if it's something real. Remember our trip to the bookshop? I didn't check once 🙂. My heart felt calm for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: Where was Kavitha when Amma took the phone for the evening?
qa.a: Kavitha was at an aunt's wedding.

qa.q: What was Kavitha afraid of while checking the phone so often?
qa.a: Kavitha was afraid the group might plan something that would be missed, feeling sure the whole world was moving on.

qa.q: What did Kavitha change that helped, and what else could Kavitha try?
qa.a: Kavitha turned off every notification except calls and asked Ayesha to ring if something was real; Kavitha could also keep meeting friends offline, as at the bookshop.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt about the request to ring if it's something real?
qa.a: Ayesha probably felt trusted and glad, since it gave a simple way to stay connected and showed the friendship mattered more than the chat.

grounding: Shows a teen checking the phone constantly from fear of missing out, then muting notifications and meeting offline.

passage:
Sahil pulled a new phone out of his bag at the bus stop and held it so the cover showed. "Got it yesterday. Also, ninety-four in physics. You?"
Keerthana had seen that quick glance after every test in their small town, checking whose face would drop. She felt a sting, then smiled. "Nice. The screen looks bright." She told him her own marks, seventy-eight, without dressing them up. "Ninety-four is a lot of work," she said, and meant it.
Then she offered him half her puffed rice from the shop by the stop. He blinked, and for a moment the game went out of him. On the bus she thought about the science-fair model she still wanted to finish, and what she cared about there.

qa.q: What marks did Sahil say he got in physics?
qa.a: He said he got ninety-four in physics.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Sahil flashed the phone and the marks, and what did she think was behind it?
qa.a: She sensed a quick glance to see whose face would drop, as if he compared to feel better than her; it stung a little, though she stayed calm. 😔

qa.q: Which choice of Keerthana's kept the moment from becoming a contest, and why?
qa.a: She answered kindly and honestly, told her marks plainly and shared her puffed rice, so she stayed warm without competing.

qa.q: Why might Sahil have blinked when offered puffed rice?
qa.a: He may have expected a contest or a sulk, and her kindness left him unsure what to do, so the game briefly went out of him.

grounding: Shows a teen sensing a friend's flaunting as comparison, staying warm, not competing, and returning to her own interests.

passage:
In the courtyard behind her mother's tailoring shop, Vandana held her phone at arm's length and frowned. The filter smoothed her cheeks and widened her eyes. Without it, the camera showed a pimple and a crooked smile, and she thought, that can't be me.
"Leave that thing, race me to the mango tree," said Madhuri, dragging her off the step. They ran until Vandana was breathless and laughing, and she noticed how far her legs had carried her.
That evening she unfollowed two accounts full of edited faces and followed a girl who posts kabaddi videos. She still looked in the mirror for a long time, but the crooked smile was at least her own.

qa.q: Whom did Vandana follow after unfollowing the two accounts of edited faces?
qa.a: She followed a girl who posts kabaddi videos.

qa.q: What did Vandana think when the camera showed her without the filter?
qa.a: She thought "that can't be me", which shows the edited image had made her real face feel wrong.

qa.q: How did racing to the mango tree help Vandana?
qa.a: It moved her attention to what her body can do, not only how it looks, and she ended up breathless and laughing.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have seen Vandana's frown at the phone?
qa.a: Madhuri may have noticed a friend being unkind to herself and chose a simple way to pull her out of it without a speech.

grounding: Shows a teen whose filtered images make her real face feel wrong, turning to real people and what her body can do.

passage:
The physics exam was at nine, and at half past midnight Madhav was still scrolling under the blanket, eyes burning, thumb moving on its own. He had said "one more video" about forty times. By morning his head ached, and he snapped at his little sister for asking him to pass the salt.
At school Shankar looked at him. "You look like you haven't slept, and you bit my head off yesterday too." Madhav admitted he couldn't stop at night.
They made a plan: the phone charges in the hall, an old clock for the alarm, a paperback by the bed. If it still didn't work, they would tell Madhav's father or the school counsellor together.
That night the hall charger blinked in the dark, and Madhav opened the book.

qa.q: Where does the phone charge under the plan Madhav and Shankar made?
qa.a: It charges in the hall.

qa.q: What might Madhav be feeling when his thumb keeps moving on its own?
qa.a: He seems unable to stop, tired and frustrated, since his eyes burn and he snaps at people the next day.

qa.q: What else could Madhav do if the plan doesn't work?
qa.a: He could tell his father or the school counsellor, as Shankar suggests, because asking for help is wise if he feels unable to change.

qa.q: How might Madhav's little sister have felt when he snapped about the salt?
qa.a: She may have felt confused or hurt, since she only asked for salt; the snap likely came from his tiredness, not from her.

grounding: Shows a teen unable to stop late-night scrolling, tired and irritable, making a phone-outside plan and a fallback of telling adults.

passage:
By lunch, the photo of Seema's clay volcano from the science fair had forty thousand views. Her phone buzzed against the desk like an insect, and each buzz made her chest bubble.
"Seema, you're famous! 🎉" Jomon said, grinning across the bench. She kept sneaking looks at the counter.
By evening it had slowed, and by night the number stood still. She felt a small dip and laughed at herself. "It was fun," she told Jomon on the walk home. "But I'm still the same person who hasn't finished her essay."
He laughed. That night she pinned a print of the volcano photo to her cupboard door and opened her notebook.

qa.q: What did Seema post that went viral?
qa.a: She posted a photo of her clay volcano from the science fair.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling with each buzz of the phone?
qa.a: Her chest bubbled with a rush of pride and excitement with every buzz. 😊

qa.q: How did Seema keep her worth separate from the numbers?
qa.a: She enjoyed it lightly, laughed at the dip when the counter stood still, and reminded herself she was still the same person with an essay to finish.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Seema's sudden fame?
qa.a: Jomon seems delighted for her and cheers her on, and her calm afterwards may show him that the number was never the point.

grounding: Shows a teen enjoying a viral post lightly without tying her worth to the numbers.

passage:
Sit, Mohit, and let me tell you how your cousin Divyansh uses that chatbot, because I watched him closely last month. I'm your Ravi Mama, remember.
He asked it to explain photosynthesis. Instead of copying the answer, he explained it back to me at dinner in his own words, and stumbled in two places. So he went to his textbook, found that the chatbot had muddled one detail, and fixed it. "It's a helper, Mama," he said. "Not the teacher, and not the answer key."
Then he asked it to check his homework, but he accepted only the corrections he could reason out himself 🙂. I said nothing. I saw a boy who wanted to learn, not just to finish.

qa.q: What did Divyansh ask the chatbot to explain?
qa.a: He asked it to explain photosynthesis.

qa.q: How does Divyansh seem to feel about the chatbot?
qa.a: Divyansh seems wary of trusting it fully and keen to learn, calling it a helper rather than the teacher and checking its answers against his textbook.

qa.q: What could Mohit copy from Divyansh's way of using the chatbot?
qa.a: Mohit could explain the topic back in Mohit's own words, check the textbook for facts, and accept only corrections that make sense after thinking them through. 👍

qa.q: How does Ravi Mama see Divyansh's approach?
qa.a: Ravi Mama sees a boy who wanted to learn rather than just finish, and he chose to watch without interfering.

grounding: Shows a teen using an AI as a helper, verifying facts and doing his own thinking.

passage:
"Who are you texting at midnight?" Akash whispered from the doorway of the room he shared with his younger sister.
"The chatbot," said Aparna. "It never judges. I told it about the fight with Diya, and my marks, and how I feel when Mummy compares me with Neha."
"You didn't tell me."
"You'd tell Mummy."
"Not if you asked me not to. But it doesn't know you, Aparna. It can't come to your school."
She was quiet. "It does help."
"Fine. Use it to sort your thoughts. But you've been low for weeks, haven't you?"
Her eyes filled. "Yes."
"Then let's tell Mummy together tomorrow. I'll sit next to you."
She nodded and closed the app.

qa.q: Who does Aparna's mother compare her with?
qa.a: Mummy compares her with Neha.

qa.q: Why does Aparna tell the chatbot things instead of Akash?
qa.a: She fears he would tell Mummy, and she likes that the chatbot never judges, so it feels safer to her than people do.

qa.q: What did Akash suggest as the next step, and why?
qa.a: He suggested they tell Mummy together the next day, with him sitting beside her, because she has been low for weeks and needs real people. 🤍

qa.q: How might Akash have felt finding Aparna awake at midnight?
qa.a: Akash seems worried and a little hurt that she hadn't told him, but he stays gentle and offers to sit beside her.

grounding: Shows a teen preferring a non-judging chatbot to people, and a sibling steering her toward telling a trusted adult.

passage:
Hi Simran,
Quick update on our history project. I asked the chatbot for sources on old trade routes and it gave me three book titles with authors and page numbers, all very confident. Yesterday I went to the school library to borrow them. Two of them don't exist, and the third is about something else. I felt silly, like I'd been lied to by someone friendly.
The librarian showed me how to search the catalogue, and we found one real book that fits. So I'm rewriting the bibliography from things I can actually hold in my hand. Could you check the dates in my section against your notes?
Thanks, Maria 🙂

qa.q: How many of the three book titles turned out not to exist?
qa.a: Two of them don't exist.

qa.q: How did Maria feel after discovering the titles were fake?
qa.a: Maria felt silly, as if lied to by someone friendly.

qa.q: What can Maria do with any chatbot answer that comes with sources?
qa.a: Maria can cross-check with books, teachers or reliable sites, using the library catalogue to see that a source exists before relying on it.

qa.q: How might the librarian see Maria's problem?
qa.a: The librarian probably sees a common mistake, since they showed Maria how to search the catalogue and helped find a real book instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a teen finding that a confident chatbot invented sources and cross-checking with the library.
